title: How do telecom companies make money, and what matters in a telecom case?
description: Telecom economics for case interviews: ARPU, churn, network investment, subscriber acquisition cost and price competition, with a worked churn example.
hook: Telecom companies make money by charging subscribers a monthly fee for mobile, broadband and TV over networks that cost enormous sums to build, so revenue is simply subscribers × average revenue per user (ARPU). Because the network is mostly a fixed cost and customers can switch fairly easily, most telecom cases come down to three things: keeping customers (churn), protecting ARPU against price competition, and deciding where new network investment pays back.
body:
How telecoms make money

Revenue = subscribers × ARPU. Around that core sit handset sales and financing, business and government contracts, and wholesale income from renting network capacity to smaller brands. Customers split into very different groups: prepaid (pay as you go, low ARPU, easy to leave), contract (higher ARPU, locked in for a period), family or bundled plans, and enterprise. Always segment before you average.

Heavy fixed investment

Spectrum licences, towers, fibre and core network equipment are huge upfront costs, and networks need constant upgrading. Once built, an extra customer costs little to serve, so filling the network is very profitable (high operating leverage). The flip side: in a market with three or four operators that all have sunk costs, each is tempted to cut prices to fill spare capacity, and price wars follow.

The measures that matter

MeasureWhat it tells you
ARPUAverage monthly revenue per subscriber
ChurnShare of subscribers leaving each month
Subscriber acquisition cost (SAC)Marketing, commissions and handset subsidy to win one customer
Capex as a share of revenueHow much the network soaks up each year

A worked example: the cost of churn

An illustrative operator has 10M subscribers paying $20 a month: $200M a month, $2.4B a year. Monthly churn rises from 1.5% to 2%, so an extra 0.5% × 10M = 50,000 customers leave each month, or 600,000 over a year.

  • Run-rate impact: by year-end, 600,000 lost customers × $20 × 12 = $144M a year of revenue gone if they are not replaced.
  • Year-one impact: smaller, because the leavers drop off gradually. Customers who leave in month 1 miss 11 months, those in month 12 miss none. 50,000 × $20 × (11 + 10 + ... + 0) = 50,000 × $20 × 66 = $66M, roughly half the run-rate.
  • Replacement cost: winning 600,000 replacements at an illustrative SAC of $150 costs $90M.

Being precise about run-rate versus in-year impact is the kind of detail interviewers notice. The cleanest way to keep it straight is a subscriber bridge: closing base = opening base + gross additions − disconnections. Run it month by month and calculate revenue on the average base. It also shows whether marketing is growing the base or only replacing leavers.

The levers

  • Retention offers at contract end, aimed at customers likely to leave rather than everyone.
  • Bundles (mobile plus broadband) that raise switching costs.
  • Network quality in the areas where churn is highest.
  • Price tiers that let price-sensitive customers trade down rather than leave, while protecting ARPU elsewhere.

Typical telecom case questions

  • Why is churn rising, and how do we reduce it?
  • We keep adding subscribers, so why is revenue falling? (a revenue drop case)
  • Should we match a rival's price cut?
  • Where should we build fibre first?

What a strong answer sounds like

Weak: "Churn is up, so we should launch a loyalty discount for all customers."
Strong: "First I'd find where churn rose: which region, tariff and tenure group. If it's concentrated where a rival just launched, it's a competitive offer. If it's spread across one region, it may be network quality. The fix is different in each case."

Common mistakes

  • Multiplying monthly losses by 12 for the year. That gives the exit run-rate, not the in-year revenue loss.
  • Blanket retention discounts. Most customers would have stayed anyway, so the discount mostly gives money away (see practice question 2).
  • Averaging across segments. Prepaid and contract customers have different ARPU, churn and acquisition costs.
  • Ignoring the network. A price response is cheap to announce, but if the root cause is coverage, it treats the symptom.

Practise

1. Subscribers grew from 20M to 22M, but annual revenue fell from $2.4B to $2.2B. What happened to monthly ARPU?

Show the answer

Before: $2.4B ÷ 20M ÷ 12 = $10.00. After: $2.2B ÷ 22M ÷ 12 = $8.33. ARPU fell about 17%. Next, ask why: price cuts, a shift to prepaid, cheaper data bundles, or customers adding second SIMs that pull the average down.

2. Each month 200,000 customers reach contract end and 20% leave. A $5-a-month discount for 12 months, offered to all of them, would cut leavers to 12%. ARPU is $25. Is it worth it?

Show the answer

Without the offer: 160,000 stay × $25 × 12 = $48M. With it: 176,000 stay × $20 × 12 = $42.24M. The offer saves 16,000 customers but loses $5.76M of revenue per monthly cohort, because 160,000 customers who would have stayed also get the discount. Even after saving 16,000 × $150 = $2.4M of replacement cost, it is negative. Target the offer at customers likely to leave.

3. Fibre costs $600 per home passed (including connection). Take-up is 40% at $40 a month with a 50% cash margin. What is payback per home passed? What if a rival builds and take-up falls to 25%?

Show the answer

Annual cash per home passed: 40% × $40 × 12 × 50% = $96, so payback is $600 ÷ $96 = 6.25 years. At 25% take-up: $60 a year, so 10 years. Being first into an area matters a lot.

Where to practise next

The Sunrise Mobile case (subscribers up, revenue down) and the Vertex Mobile case (a 6% revenue fall) practise diagnosis. The Saltire Telecom case is about where to build fibre when a rival is coming. For the maths of payback, see payback and NPV.
